name: p5.js
what: A beginner-friendly JavaScript library for drawing, animation and interaction in the browser; the most used library on Art Blocks.
firstProject: Draw 100 random lines from one seed; change the seed and see a new output. That is long-form generative art in miniature.
intro: p5.js is a free JavaScript library for drawing, animating and responding to input in a web page. It grew out of Processing, the 'sketchbook' language made for artists, and it is the most used library on Art Blocks. You write a short program, give it a random seed, and every seed draws a different work.

history.text: Casey Reas and Ben Fry start Processing at the MIT Media Lab, a programming language meant for visual artists.
Lauren Lee McCarthy creates p5.js, bringing Processing's ideas to JavaScript and the browser.

steps: Open the p5.js web editor (editor.p5js.org) and run the default sketch; no install needed.
Follow the first Coding Train p5.js videos: shapes, colour, variables, loops.
Replace Math.random with a seeded random number generator so one seed always draws the same picture.
Read Art Blocks' 'building your project' page to see how tokenData.hash becomes your seed.
Make 20 outputs from 20 seeds and print them on one sheet; keep the rules that surprise you.
starterCost: Free: p5.js is free and open-source software [sourced: p5js.org]. A laptop you already own is enough.
humanity: The hand: scan one of your own pencil lines and let the code draw with its wobble instead of a perfect curve.
Imperfection: add a small, seeded tremble to every stroke, so no two outputs share the same 'steadiness'.
Collaboration: invite someone who has never coded to choose the rules while you type, and credit them on the token.
Time: let a sketch slowly erase and redraw itself, the way a drawing on a chalkboard fades between classes.

name: WebGL / GLSL shaders
what: Programs that run on the graphics card, colouring every pixel in parallel; fast, dense, and a third of Art Blocks projects.
firstProject: Write a fragment shader that maps a noise field to a two-colour palette, then feed it a seed.
intro: Shaders are small programs that run on the graphics card and decide the colour of every pixel at once. GLSL is the language they are written in, and WebGL is how browsers run them. They make dense, fast, glowing images and are behind about a third of Art Blocks projects in our data.

history.text: GLSL becomes part of core OpenGL with OpenGL 2.0, making programmable shading standard on graphics cards.
WebGL 1.0 is released, bringing GPU shaders into the web browser.

steps: Work through the first chapters of The Book of Shaders in its live editor.
Write a fragment shader that colours the screen by x and y, then add time.
Add a noise function and map its value to a two-colour palette.
Pass a seed from JavaScript as a uniform so each token gets its own field.
Check your shader on a phone: precision and speed differ by device.
starterCost: Free: browsers include WebGL; The Book of Shaders is free to read online [sourced: thebookofshaders.com].
humanity: Imperfection: GPUs make perfect gradients; add grain, dust and uneven edges so the image feels made, not rendered.
Memory: sample the colours of a photo you care about and let the shader build its palette from them.
The body: drive one uniform from slow breathing (a 4-second in, 6-second out cycle) so the image breathes with a person.
Place: use the sky colour at a real location and hour as the base of the palette.

what: Vector output: shapes as paths, which plotters, cutters and embroidery software can read.

Imperfection: keep stroke order visible, so the viewer can see how the line was made.

name: Live network fetch in script
what: Scripts that pull live data from the web when they render.
firstProject: Fetch one public value (for example a block number) and let it nudge a parameter; render a fallback when offline.
intro: Some Art Blocks scripts fetch live data from the web when they render, so the work can change with the world. It is powerful but fragile: if the source goes away, the work must still render.

history.text: Jesse James Garrett's article (Feb 18, 2005) coins the term Ajax for web pages that fetch data in the background.

steps: Fetch one public value (for example the latest block number) and let it nudge one parameter.
Always include a fallback render when offline.
Cache nothing private; never send viewer data anywhere.
Write in the description what is fetched and from where.
starterCost: Free for public APIs; some data providers charge [estimate].
humanity: Place: read the weather of one town and let it set the mood of the piece.
Care: tie the work to a public good (a river level, an air reading) so watching it means watching over something.
Memory: if the source disappears, freeze the last state as a record of when it stopped.

intro: AI models used to make or run the work: training on your own images, or running a small model in the browser. On Art Blocks, Mario Klingemann and Sofia Crespo have released AI-based projects (2023 in our data).

history.text: Harold Cohen begins AARON, an early program that made drawings on its own.
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are introduced, later widely used by artists.

steps: Run a pretrained ml5.js model in the browser on your own drawing.
Train a tiny model only on your own images; write down what went in.
Let the model's output steer one parameter, not the whole image.
Credit data sources in the description.

Stream one signal into a sketch and smooth it heavily.

Map it to one parameter, like density.

name: Pen plotters
what: A machine that draws your vector output with real pens.
firstProject: Export one SVG from your sketch, optimise it with vpype and plot it on A4.
intro: A pen plotter is a machine that draws with a real pen, following vector paths. It is the 'house' physical format of on-chain generative art: Tyler Hobbs's Fidenza (2021) and Licia He's Running Moon are verified plotter works in our data, and Plottables is a platform built for it.

history.text: Georg Nees and others show some of the first computer drawings made on plotters.
Earliest first mint on the Plottables contract (plotter-first generative art on Art Blocks technology) in our data: Streamlines by NumbersInMotion.

steps: Make your sketch output SVG paths.
Clean the SVG with vpype: merge lines, sort for travel, remove duplicates.
Plot on a borrowed or hobby plotter (AxiDraw or similar) with one pen.
Try three papers and two pens; keep notes.
Decide how a token holder gets a plot, and record it.
starterCost: A hobby plotter costs a few hundred dollars; makerspaces often have one [estimate].
humanity: The hand: let pen pressure, ink bleed and paper tooth finish what the code started.
Imperfection: Licia He makes plotter paintings and calls her plotters robots (per her site); let paint skip and pool.
Time: a plot can take hours; film it and share the slowness.
Care: sign and date each plot by hand.
gotcha: Clean the SVG with vpype: merge lines, sort for travel, remove duplicates.

Care: pick paper that will outlive you.

name: Risograph
what: A stencil duplicator with spot-colour drums; cheap per sheet.
firstProject: Export each colour as its own greyscale layer and run 10 different outputs.
intro: Risograph is a stencil-based printer that prints in bright soy inks, one colour at a time, with a grainy, imperfect look. Pandelune's Reverie (2024) is the Art Blocks example in our map.

history.text: Riso Kagaku Corporation introduces the Risograph in Japan.

steps: Split your output into 2–3 colours.
Export one grayscale file per colour.
Book a riso studio (many cities have one).
Print a small zine of outputs.
starterCost: A riso studio run costs tens of dollars [estimate].
humanity: Imperfection: riso grain and offset are the point.
Collaboration: make a zine with friends, one page each.
Memory: print a small run and give it away by hand.
gotcha: Print a small zine of outputs.

name: Darkroom / film / cyanotype
what: Light-sensitive processes such as cyanotype prints from digital negatives.
firstProject: Print your output as a transparency and make a cyanotype in sunlight.
intro: Darkroom, film and cyanotype processes make images with light and chemistry. Dmitri Cherniak's Light Years (2022) and Trevor Paglen's PRELUDES connect this tradition to tokens.

history.text: John Herschel discovers the cyanotype process.
Anna Atkins publishes Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions, often called the first book illustrated with photographs.

steps: Print your output as a transparency (an inkjet negative).
Coat paper with cyanotype chemistry (kits are sold online).
Expose in sunlight, rinse in water.
Scan the result and compare to the screen.
starterCost: A cyanotype kit costs under fifty dollars [estimate].
humanity: Time: sunlight sets the exposure; the day's weather becomes part of the work.
The hand: brush marks from coating stay on the paper.
Place: expose under the sun of a place that matters to you.
Imperfection: no two prints match; that is the edition.
gotcha: Scan the result and compare to the screen.

Convert it to a stitch file with Ink/Stitch (free Inkscape extension).

Memory: embroider on fabric that belonged to someone.
Collaboration: send the file to an embroiderer and credit them.
gotcha: Stitch one test on a home embroidery machine or at a makerspace.

Check it in a slicer (Cura, PrusaSlicer).
Print small first.
Decide how owners get files or prints.

humanity: The hand: finish prints by sanding or painting.

Care: print in a material you would want to keep.
